title: Robust Agent Teams via Socially-Attentive Monitoring
review_status: full-text audit complete; JAIR publication chronology, monitoring-selectivity definitions and theorem conditions, ModSAF/RoboCup empirical scope, diagnosis and task-performance limitations checked
sections_checked: Title page and publication metadata: JAIR 12 (2000), pp. 105–147
Abstract/introduction and Sections 2–3: selectivity problem, team-monitoring model and domains
Sections 4–5: centralized and distributed monitoring guarantees; key-agent and observability assumptions
Sections 6–9: empirical applications, diagnosis, related work, conclusion and open task-performance relation
venue_year_verified: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, volume 12 (2000), pages 105–147; arXiv first submitted 2011-06-01
evidence_note: The article proves sound-and-complete distributed teamwork-failure detection under stated simple-team/observability conditions while monitoring key agents, and studies a framework in ModSAF and RoboCup-related settings. This is not an unrestricted guarantee for arbitrary team structures or partial-observation regimes; the paper leaves the relationship between its team-quality metric and task performance open.

venue_year_verified: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, volume 17 (2002), pages 171–228; arXiv first submitted 2011-06-22
evidence_note: E-Elves ran for ten research-group users from June–December 2000, usually 5–10 Friday agents per user, and monitored nearly 700 meetings. The paper reports real system usage and strategy/model correspondence, not a randomized counterfactual user-outcome trial. A 2009 RIAACT follow-up tests time-critical/interruptible strategies in a disaster-response simulation and shows the benefit can reverse when the probability that inconsistency resolution helps is low.

review_status: full-text audit complete; updated-CNP task-change mechanism, JADE/FIPA-ACL and JATLite/KQML implementation, five-task/two-change comparison, results and stated future work checked
sections_checked: Abstract and introduction: in-flight task modification motivation

venue_year_verified: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications, volume 4, issue 11 (2013), DOI 10.14569/IJACSA.2013.041106; arXiv first submitted 2013-12-16
evidence_note: The paper compares a task-change-capable updated-CNP to conventional CNP in a predator–prey implementation across JADE/FIPA-ACL and JATLite/KQML. Its described example has five tasks and two changed during execution; it reports quicker accommodation qualitatively but provides no broad application-level replication. Its own future work names application-specific evaluation, scalability, fairness, robustness and related limits.

title: Improving Adjustable Autonomy Strategies for Time-Critical Domains
review_status: targeted primary-source full-text follow-up; continuous-time/interruptible policies, disaster-response simulation, run-averaged outcomes, significance, and sensitivity to inconsistency-resolution utility checked
sections_checked: Abstract and Sections 1–3: RIAACT model, continuous-time policy and interruptible actions
Section 4: policy and DEFACTO simulation experiments
Results: 50-run averages, comparison to baseline, significance and P(IU) sensitivity
Conclusion: generalization limits and future work
evidence_note: RIAACT extends adjustable autonomy with inconsistency resolution and continuous-time interruptible actions in a disaster-response simulation. It reports 50-run averages and a statistically significant comparison (reported p=0.0163), but also finds that at P(IU)=0.3 the method can do worse than Always Accept for a reported response-time setting. Benefit depends on calibration of whether resolving a disagreement helps.

title: Task Assignment of the Improved Contract Net Protocol under a Multi-Agent System
review_status: targeted primary-source 13-page journal full text; protocol distinction, simulation sizes, comparison statistics/table, strengths and stated limitations/future work checked
sections_checked: Sections 1–3: ICNP pheromone/response-threshold mechanism and relation to prior CNP variants
Section 4 and Sections 5.1–5.3: Repast experiments varying task and agent counts; protocol comparisons
Table 2: 30-agent, 1,000-task, Lmax=3 error and completion outcomes
Section 6: redundant-information limitation and future research
evidence_note: This is adjacent evidence, not a replication of the sampled 2013 in-flight task-modification rule. It compares a pheromone/response-threshold protocol to classical and dynamic CNP in synthetic Repast simulations. At 30 agents, 1,000 tasks and Lmax=3, the authors report completion of 86.7%/93.2%/100% respectively and 11 ICNP errors successfully re-forwarded. They acknowledge redundant shared-environment messages may lower efficiency and identify bidding/assignment constraints as future work.
